cards.scenario: Developers federate via AD; allow RDS only in us-east-1, other services unrestricted, minimal operational burden.
cards.ok: SAML federation to IAM role with PowerUserAccess plus customer-managed policy denying RDS outside us-east-1.
cards.bad: SAML role with AdministrativeAccess plus customer-managed policy denying RDS outside us-east-1.
cards.why: AdministrativeAccess gives far more than least privilege; PowerUserAccess keeps developer productivity while the explicit deny restricts RDS to us-east-1.

cards.scenario: Select three correct facts about Service Control Policies in AWS Organizations.
cards.ok: SCPs affect all users, roles and the root user, do not affect service-linked roles, and block actions IAM allows.
cards.bad: SCPs affect service-linked roles and exclude the root user, and IAM allow still permits denied actions.
cards.why: SCPs set maximum permissions, so IAM allows cannot override them; they apply to root users of member accounts but never to service-linked roles.

cards.scenario: Two VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs must reach a hard-coded MySQL IP privately with minimal maintenance.
cards.ok: Create VPC peering and add routes in both VPC route tables to the other VPC's CIDR range.
cards.bad: Attach internet gateways to both VPCs, default routes, and an Elastic IP on the MySQL instance.
cards.why: Peering with routes in both directions gives private connectivity with the existing IP; internet or Elastic IP paths are insecure and need app changes.

cards.scenario: Centrally managed VPCs shared across accounts in an AWS Organization for highly interconnected applications.
cards.ok: Use VPC sharing to share one or more subnets with other accounts in the organization.
cards.bad: Use VPC sharing to share an entire VPC with other accounts in the organization.
cards.why: VPC sharing works at the subnet level through Resource Access Manager; you cannot share a whole VPC, and peering does not share subnets.

cards.scenario: Private hosted zone associated with a VPC, but domain names do not resolve.
cards.ok: Enable both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution on the VPC.
cards.bad: Fix the NS and SOA records so they have the correct configuration.
cards.why: Private hosted zones are resolved only by the Amazon-provided VPC DNS server, so enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames must be on.

cards.scenario: Many VPCs across accounts need access to services; cost-effective, quick and secure.
cards.ok: Use centralized VPC endpoints in a shared services VPC for connecting multiple VPCs.
cards.bad: Use a transit VPC to reduce cost and share the resources across VPCs.
cards.why: A shared services VPC with centralized endpoints is cheaper and simpler than transit VPC appliances or full-mesh peering or Direct Connect.

cards.scenario: Bidirectional DNS resolution between on-premises network and AWS VPC.
cards.ok: Create an outbound Resolver endpoint to forward VPC queries on premises, and an inbound endpoint for on-premises resolvers to forward queries into the VPC.
cards.bad: Create an inbound endpoint to forward VPC queries on premises, and an outbound endpoint for on-premises resolvers to send queries into the VPC.
cards.why: Inbound endpoints receive queries from on-premises resolvers; outbound endpoints forward VPC queries out. Directions are swapped in the wrong choice, and universal endpoint does not exist.

cards.scenario: Hybrid network, no NAT, highly available, high bandwidth for multi-Region deployment after migration.
cards.ok: Direct Connect to each data center from different providers with routing failover to the other data center's connection.
cards.bad: Direct Connect as primary for all data centers with a VPN backup using the same virtual private gateway and BGP.
cards.why: Maximum resiliency uses separate Direct Connect connections from different providers in more than one location; a VPN backup lacks high bandwidth.

cards.scenario: HQ on Direct Connect, two branches on Site-to-Site VPN must exchange data with each other and HQ.
cards.ok: Set up AWS VPN CloudHub through the virtual private gateway so all sites communicate.
cards.bad: Set up VPC peering between the branch offices and corporate headquarters.
cards.why: VPN CloudHub links multiple VPN and Direct Connect sites via one virtual private gateway; VPC peering and endpoints do not connect on-premises sites.

cards.scenario: Serverless document upload app must give low latency to customers in any Region.
cards.ok: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and switch API Gateway Regional endpoints to edge-optimized endpoints.
cards.bad: Change API Gateway Regional endpoints to private API endpoints and use CloudFront signed URLs.
cards.why: Edge-optimized endpoints and Transfer Acceleration route users through CloudFront edge locations; private endpoints are VPC-only and signed URLs only control access.

cards.scenario: Restrict a single installer download and a whole members' area to paying subscribers via CloudFront.
cards.ok: Use signed URLs for the single installation file and signed cookies for all files in the members' area.
cards.bad: Use signed cookies for the single installation file and signed URLs for all files in the members' area.
cards.why: Signed URLs suit one individual file or clients without cookie support; signed cookies grant access to multiple restricted files without changing URLs.

cards.scenario: Redesign 99.99% SLA global game app for scalability and automatic failover at lowest cost.
cards.ok: Route 53 latency routing with health checks, S3, API Gateway and Lambda, and DynamoDB global tables with DAX.
cards.bad: Route 53 geolocation routing with health checks, NLB with Fargate containers, and Aurora Global Database.
cards.why: Serverless S3, Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB global tables scale and fail over at lowest cost; latency routing also fixes the latency complaints.

cards.scenario: Global offices see poor latency uploading and downloading 100 MB S3 videos; keep serverless storage (select two).
cards.ok: Put CloudFront in front of the S3 bucket, and enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
cards.bad: Create S3 buckets in every office Region, or run EC2 with a daily job copying data to EBS volumes.
cards.why: CloudFront and S3 Transfer Acceleration use edge locations to speed both uploads and downloads while staying serverless; EFS, EC2 and EBS are not serverless.

cards.scenario: CloudFront content types that skip the regional edge cache and go directly to the origin (select two).
cards.ok: Proxy methods PUT/POST/PATCH/OPTIONS/DELETE, and dynamic content with a behavior forwarding all headers.
cards.bad: Static content like style sheets and JavaScript, and e-commerce assets such as product photos.
cards.why: Proxy methods and dynamic content (all headers forwarded) bypass regional edge caches; cacheable static assets and media flow through them.

cards.scenario: Test blue-green for global mobile app in two days on as many users as possible despite DNS caching.
cards.ok: Use Global Accelerator traffic dials and endpoint weights to shift traffic, effective within seconds.
cards.bad: Use Route 53 weighted routing to spread traffic across the deployments.
cards.why: Global Accelerator uses static anycast IPs, so it ignores DNS caching; Route 53 weighting is delayed by cached answers, and ELB is not global.

cards.scenario: Launch configurations with default tenancy used in a dedicated-tenancy VPC versus dedicated tenancy in a default VPC.
cards.ok: Instances from both LC-A and LC-B launch with dedicated tenancy.
cards.bad: LC-A instances get dedicated tenancy while LC-B instances get default tenancy.
cards.why: Dedicated tenancy set on the launch configuration or on the VPC results in dedicated instances; either setting being dedicated wins.

cards.scenario: Migrate on-premises Chef or Puppet workflows with minimal change and less operational overhead.
cards.ok: Replatform to AWS using OpsWorks as the configuration management service for server configuration.
cards.bad: Rehost to AWS using OpsWorks as the configuration management service for server configuration.
cards.why: Moving to managed OpsWorks Chef or Puppet leverages cloud optimizations without changing core architecture, which is replatforming rather than plain rehosting.

cards.scenario: Select three key considerations when using Lambda as the serverless backbone.
cards.ok: Use Lambda Layers for shared code, NAT for VPC-enabled internet access, and CloudWatch alarms on concurrency or invocations.
cards.bad: Package dependencies separately for cold starts, and over-provision function timeout for proper performance.
cards.why: Memory, not timeout, drives compute power, and AWS advises smaller packages rather than split dependency packages; databases cannot be installed on Lambda.

cards.scenario: Faster Lambda deployments plus quicker error detection and rollback for CloudFront, API Gateway, Lambda stack.
cards.ok: Use SAM traffic shifting via CodeDeploy with pre-traffic and post-traffic test functions; roll back on CloudWatch alarms.
cards.bad: Use nested CloudFormation stacks with change sets and roll back the change set when the function errors out.
cards.why: CodeDeploy tests pre-traffic and shifts gradually with alarm rollback, so errors are detected early; CloudFormation change sets reveal failures only after deployment.

cards.scenario: ASG across two AZs: AZs unbalanced after manual terminations; one instance fails ALB health check.
cards.ok: Rebalancing launches new instances before terminating old ones; unhealthy instance is terminated first, then replaced in a later activity.
cards.bad: Rebalancing terminates old instances before launching new; unhealthy instance is replaced first, then terminated afterwards.
cards.why: Rebalancing is launch-before-terminate to preserve availability, but health-check replacement terminates first and then launches, in separate scaling activities.

cards.scenario: Video uploads to EFS scanned periodically cause unreliability and redundant processing; improve reliability and remove duplicates.
cards.ok: Upload to S3, S3 trigger invokes Lambda to queue link and instructions in SQS, workers scale on queue depth.
cards.bad: Upload to S3, EventBridge triggers Lambda to queue in SQS, workers scale on queue depth.
cards.why: The S3 trigger to Lambda to SQS pattern with queue-depth scaling fits; the other queue options differ only in trigger, and Lambda-only processing is limited for large videos.

cards.scenario: Migrate hundreds of idle PoC PHP, JavaScript, Python web apps with lowest infrastructure cost and least development effort.
cards.ok: Dockerize each application and run on an ECS cluster behind an ALB with dynamic port mapping.
cards.bad: Create AMIs from each VM with Server Migration Service and run each app on a dedicated EC2 instance.
cards.why: ALB dynamic port mapping packs many containers per instance, lowering cost; dedicated instances per low-traffic app cost more and serverless needs major rewrites.

cards.scenario: RDS Multi-AZ versus Read Replica replication capabilities.
cards.ok: Multi-AZ is synchronous across at least two AZs; Read Replicas are asynchronous and can be same-AZ, cross-AZ or cross-Region.
cards.bad: Multi-AZ is asynchronous across two AZs; Read Replicas are asynchronous and can be same-AZ, cross-AZ or cross-Region.
cards.why: Multi-AZ synchronously replicates to a standby for durability and failover; Read Replicas use asynchronous replication for read scaling.

cards.scenario: Scale web tier and Aurora PostgreSQL layer based on user traffic.
cards.ok: ALB with round robin and sticky sessions, plus Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas with EC2 Auto Scaling group.
cards.bad: Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Writes with EC2 Auto Scaling group behind the load balancer.
cards.why: Aurora Auto Scaling adds Aurora Replicas only, not writers; NLB has no least-outstanding-requests algorithm and ALB has no flow hash.

cards.scenario: Buffer and transform streaming JSON events with dynamic schemas, with real-time dashboards.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Firehose with Lambda transform delivering to OpenSearch, using its Kibana dashboards for near-real-time visualization.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Firehose with Lambda transform delivering to an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster for visualization.
cards.why: OpenSearch handles semi-structured JSON with dynamic schemas and includes dashboards; relational Aurora needs fixed schemas and Athena is not real-time.

cards.scenario: Relational DB read-heavy with global branch offices; keep schema, MOST cost-effective and high performance.
cards.ok: Use Amazon Aurora Global Database for fast local reads with low latency in each Region.
cards.bad: Use Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables for fast local reads and writes in each Region.
cards.why: Must keep the relational schema; DynamoDB is NoSQL and Redshift is analytic, while Aurora Global Database keeps the relational model with cross-Region replicas.

cards.scenario: Analytics reports slow down the RDS MySQL SaaS app; MOST cost-optimal fix.
cards.ok: Create a Read Replica in the same Region as the primary and point the analytics workload there.
cards.bad: Create a Read Replica in another Region for disaster recovery and point the analytics workload there.
cards.why: A same-Region replica offloads reads without cross-Region transfer cost; the Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads and Lambda does not fix the DB load.

cards.scenario: Decoupled order processing must scale for traffic spikes writing to DynamoDB; MOST reliable.
cards.ok: Ingest orders into an SQS queue and trigger a Lambda function to process them.
cards.bad: Push orders to an SNS topic and subscribe a Lambda function to process them.
cards.why: SQS durably buffers orders until Lambda processes them, so spikes are not lost; SNS pushes directly and failures risk dropped messages.

cards.scenario: Index first 250 bytes of 100,000 S3 objects totaling 50 TB into Elasticsearch MOST efficiently.
cards.ok: Issue a Byte Range Fetch for the first 250 bytes, or use S3 Select ScanRange, and load results into Elasticsearch.
cards.bad: Read each entire file, extract the first 250 bytes, and store that information in Elasticsearch.
cards.why: Byte-range and ScanRange retrieval transfer only 250 bytes per object instead of 50 TB; no built-in Elasticsearch import or DMS path indexes S3 files.

cards.scenario: Kinesis Agent sends VPC flow log data to a Firehose stream sourced from Kinesis Data Streams; data not arriving.
cards.ok: Kinesis Agent cannot write to a Firehose delivery stream whose source is already set to Kinesis Data Streams.
cards.bad: Kinesis Agent can only write to Kinesis Data Streams, not to Kinesis Firehose.
cards.why: The agent supports both services, but a Firehose stream with a Kinesis Data Streams source accepts data only from that stream, rejecting direct PUT.

cards.scenario: 429 errors with Lambda never invoked; need separate quota for premium customers.
cards.ok: Cause is the account-level API Gateway calls-per-second limit; use API keys with usage plans for per-client throttling for premium customers.
cards.bad: Cause is the account per-method API Gateway limit; use API keys with usage plans for per-client throttling for premium customers.
cards.why: 429 with no Lambda invocation means API Gateway account-level throttling, not a per-method limit; usage plans with API keys give per-client quotas.

cards.scenario: API Gateway must support both stateful and stateless client-server communication.
cards.ok: REST APIs are stateless; WebSocket APIs give stateful, full-duplex communication.
cards.bad: REST APIs are stateful; WebSocket APIs give stateless, full-duplex communication.
cards.why: REST is HTTP-based and stateless, while WebSocket keeps a persistent connection and is therefore stateful; the swapped options reverse this.

cards.scenario: Move year-old Redshift data to S3 yet still cross-reference it with daily Redshift reports.
cards.ok: Use Redshift Spectrum tables pointing at the S3 historical data and query alongside Redshift tables.
cards.bad: Query the historical data with Athena and export flat files to cross-reference with Redshift reports.
cards.why: Spectrum queries S3 data in place and joins it with Redshift tables without loading or manual exports; Athena cannot join directly with Redshift.

cards.scenario: Compare Multi-AZ and Read Replica behavior of RDS MySQL versus Aurora MySQL (select three).
cards.ok: Multi-AZ synchronous in both; upgrades hit all instances together; RDS replica promotes to standalone, Aurora replica promotes to primary.
cards.bad: Aurora Multi-AZ is synchronous while RDS Multi-AZ is asynchronous; RDS replica promotes to primary while Aurora replica promotes to standalone.
cards.why: RDS Multi-AZ standby is synchronous too; Aurora replicas become the primary on failover while RDS replicas are promoted to standalone instances.

cards.scenario: Log all DynamoDB item changes in near real-time to detect anomalies with minimal custom development.
cards.ok: DynamoDB Streams to Lambda to Kinesis Data Streams, then Kinesis Data Analytics detects anomalies and SNS notifies.
cards.bad: DynamoDB Streams to Lambda writing directly to Kinesis Data Analytics, then SNS notifies.
cards.why: KDA reads from a streaming source such as Kinesis Data Streams, so Lambda cannot output records directly to KDA; CloudTrail does not capture item-level changes.

cards.scenario: KDS has multiple consumers with a lag between producers and consumers; improve delivery performance.
cards.ok: Use Kinesis Data Streams enhanced fan-out so each consumer gets its own 2 MB/s per shard.
cards.bad: Replace Kinesis Data Streams with SQS FIFO queues for the required read throughput.
cards.why: Shared 2 MB/s per shard is split across consumers; enhanced fan-out gives each consumer a dedicated pipe, whereas swapping services does not fit.

cards.scenario: Oracle to Aurora MySQL via DMS, minimal source impact, validate data accuracy before cutover.
cards.ok: Enable DMS data validation on the migration task to compare source and target data and report mismatches.
cards.bad: Enable DMS premigration assessment on the task to compare source and target data and report mismatches.
cards.why: Data validation compares migrated rows; premigration assessment only checks for issues before the task runs, and table metrics only show statistics.

cards.scenario: Fully serverless sensor ingestion with no manual capacity provisioning, writing to DynamoDB.
cards.ok: SQS standard queue polled in batches by Lambda, writing to auto-scaled DynamoDB.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Stream polled by an EC2 application, writing to auto-scaled DynamoDB.
cards.why: SQS plus Lambda needs no provisioning, while EC2 consumers and manually sized shards are not serverless; Firehose cannot write directly to DynamoDB.

cards.scenario: Real-time clickstream capture with HA that feeds multiple independent downstream applications simultaneously.
cards.ok: Kinesis Data Streams lets multiple applications consume the same stream concurrently and independently.
cards.bad: Kinesis Data Firehose lets applications consume the same stream concurrently and independently.
cards.why: KDS supports multiple consumers with ordering and replay; Firehose only loads to destinations and SQS messages are consumed once.

cards.scenario: Live gaming leaderboard needing in-memory speed, high availability and single-digit millisecond latency (select two).
cards.ok: ElastiCache for Redis, or DynamoDB with DAX as the in-memory cache.
cards.bad: Plain DynamoDB, or RDS Aurora, as the in-memory leaderboard store.
cards.why: Redis and DAX are in-memory; DynamoDB alone is not in-memory, Aurora is relational and Neptune is a graph database.

cards.scenario: Hold delivery of only certain SQS messages (sensitive photos) back by one minute.
cards.ok: Use message timers to set a per-message one-minute delay.
cards.bad: Use delay queues to postpone delivery by one minute.
cards.why: A delay queue delays all new messages in the queue, while message timers delay individual messages; visibility timeout applies only after receipt.

cards.scenario: Ordered SQS processing at 2,400 messages per second, most cost-effective.
cards.ok: Use an SQS FIFO queue with batches of 8 messages per operation.
cards.bad: Use an SQS FIFO queue with batches of 4 messages per operation.
cards.why: FIFO allows 300 operations per second, so 300 x 8 = 2,400 messages per second; batches of 4 reach only 1,200 per second.

cards.scenario: Overseas sites upload large video files to S3 slowly; MOST cost-effective speed-up.
cards.ok: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration together with multipart uploads for the large files.
cards.bad: Use AWS Global Accelerator together with multipart uploads for the large files.
cards.why: Transfer Acceleration is the S3 feature using CloudFront edge locations; Direct Connect or VPN cost more and Global Accelerator does not accelerate S3 uploads.

cards.scenario: Shared POSIX file system tier plus block storage tier needing more than a million IOPS.
cards.ok: EFS for the shared POSIX data tier and EC2 Instance Store for the million-plus IOPS service tier.
cards.bad: EFS for the shared POSIX data tier and Provisioned IOPS EBS volumes for the service tier.
cards.why: EBS provisioned IOPS tops out well below a million per volume; instance store delivers over a million IOPS, and EFS provides shared POSIX.

cards.scenario: 15 instances with 3 TB gp2 volumes need 3,000 more IOPS each; MOST cost-efficient.
cards.ok: Increase each gp2 volume from 3 TB to 4 TB to gain the extra baseline IOPS.
cards.bad: Change each volume from gp2 to io1 with 12,000 provisioned IOPS.
cards.why: gp2 gives 3 IOPS per GB, so 4 TB yields 12,000 IOPS with no migration; io1 provisioned IOPS costs more.

cards.scenario: Redshift cluster must be restorable in another Region within five hours, cost-effectively.
cards.ok: Use CloudFormation StackSets for the cluster template and enable cross-Region snapshot copy; restore from snapshot during disaster.
cards.bad: Run two identical clusters in different Regions with Kinesis Data Streams feeding both clusters.
cards.why: Cross-Region snapshots with restore meet a five-hour RTO cheaply; a running secondary cluster is far costlier and Redshift is not multi-AZ via Auto Scaling.

cards.scenario: Migrate very large data set to S3 fastest with 500 Mbps Direct Connect and 1 Gbps VPN available.
cards.ok: Order three Snowball Edge appliances, split the data across them and ship to AWS for copy to S3.
cards.bad: Leverage the 1 Gbps IPSec VPN connection to transfer the data to S3 over the public internet.
cards.why: At this data volume the network links would take far too long; shipping Snowball Edge devices is much faster than 500 Mbps or 1 Gbps links.

cards.scenario: Robust DR plan for Amazon RDS databases; choose three correct facts.
cards.ok: Manual snapshots copy or share across Regions and accounts, backups and replicas work cross-Region, and RTO means time to recover.
cards.bad: Read Replica failover is automatic like Multi-AZ, and automated snapshots can be shared with up to 20 accounts.
cards.why: RTO is recovery time, not data loss; Read Replica promotion is manual and automated snapshots must be copied to manual snapshots before sharing.

cards.scenario: Rank monthly charges for storing a 5 GB file on S3 Standard, EFS Standard and 50 GB gp2 EBS.
cards.ok: S3 Standard is cheapest, then EFS, and EBS costs the most.
cards.bad: EBS is cheapest, then S3 Standard, and EFS costs the most.
cards.why: EBS bills provisioned 50 GB at $0.10 = $5; EFS bills used 5 GB at $0.30 = $1.50; S3 Standard is about $0.023 per GB.

cards.scenario: Archive 9 PB on-premises data to durable long-term storage quickly and MOST cost-optimally.
cards.ok: Use multiple Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices, import into S3 and apply a lifecycle policy to Glacier.
cards.bad: Use a Snowmobile, import into S3 and apply a lifecycle policy to transition the data to Glacier.
cards.why: Snowmobile is intended for exabyte-scale transfers beyond 10 PB; 9 PB fits Snowball Edge, and Snowball imports go to S3 first, not directly into Glacier.

cards.scenario: Data lake grows 2 TB daily per zone; Athena queries only curated zone; MOST cost-optimal.
cards.ok: Lifecycle-transition raw zone to Glacier Deep Archive after 1 day, and write curated data in a compressed format.
cards.bad: Lifecycle-transition curated zone to Glacier Deep Archive after 1 day, and write curated data as CSV.
cards.why: Raw data is rarely read, so archive it; curated data must stay queryable by Athena, and compressed columnar formats cut storage and scan cost versus CSV.

cards.scenario: Hybrid archive: only frequently accessed results cached locally, all results backed up in S3.
cards.ok: Use Volume Gateway cached volumes storing the full volume in S3 and keeping frequently accessed data cached locally.
cards.bad: Use Volume Gateway stored volumes keeping the full volume locally and asynchronously backing up the data to S3.
cards.why: Cached volumes keep primary data in S3 with a local cache of hot data; stored volumes keep the whole data set on premises.

cards.scenario: Archive in S3 Glacier must enforce regulatory compliance controls (WORM) on archived data.
cards.ok: Store in a Glacier vault and enforce compliance with a Vault Lock policy.
cards.bad: Store in Glacier vault but enforce compliance with an S3 Access Control List.
cards.why: Vault Lock policies deploy WORM-style compliance controls; ACLs only manage access and lifecycle policies only transition or expire objects.

cards.scenario: Nightly backups in two Regions, instant restore in Production, restore within 24 hours in DR, MOST cost-effective.
cards.ok: Replicate S3 Standard to S3 Standard in the DR Region, then lifecycle immediately to Glacier.
cards.bad: Replicate S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA in the DR Region, then lifecycle immediately to Glacier.
cards.why: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum before transition to Glacier, so it cannot move immediately; Standard to Glacier is allowed and cheaper.

cards.scenario: Migrate hundreds of TB to S3 online, then give on-premises apps low-latency access; MOST performant.
cards.ok: Use DataSync for the bulk migration to S3, then File Gateway for low-latency ongoing access.
cards.bad: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for the migration, then DataSync for low-latency ongoing access.
cards.why: DataSync accelerates bulk online transfers while File Gateway caches locally for low latency; DataSync is not an access layer and TA is not a migration tool.

cards.scenario: Migrate blog web servers to AWS over Direct Connect; authors keep updating shared NAS content without delay.
cards.ok: Attach an EFS file system to on-premises servers as the NAS, and mount the same EFS on AWS web servers.
cards.bad: Replace the NAS with an on-premises file gateway and mount the same gateway bucket on EC2 web servers.
cards.why: EFS is accessible on premises over Direct Connect and from EC2 concurrently so updates are instant; a file gateway bucket cannot be mounted directly by EC2.

cards.scenario: Transfer 140 TB monthly over idle 10 Gbps Direct Connect private VIF by Monday; LEAST expensive.
cards.ok: Configure a public virtual interface on the Direct Connect connection and copy the data to S3 over it.
cards.bad: Order multiple Snowball Edge appliances, load data in parallel, and ship them to AWS to copy into S3.
cards.why: About 3.6 TB per hour fits 140 TB in the 2-day window, so Snowball cost is unnecessary; S3 is reached through a public VIF, not a private VIF.

cards.scenario: Automate and accelerate online transfers of hundreds of TB into S3, EFS and FSx for Windows File Server.
cards.ok: Use AWS DataSync, which natively integrates with S3, EFS and FSx for Windows File Server.
cards.bad: Use AWS Transfer Family to automate and accelerate online transfers to these storage services.
cards.why: DataSync automates and accelerates bulk online copy to those three services; Snowball is offline and File Gateway only fronts S3 or FSx.

cards.scenario: Prevent anyone launching an EC2 instance in another VPC from reading private S3 artifacts.
cards.ok: Create an S3 VPC endpoint and a bucket policy allowing access only from that VPC endpoint.
cards.bad: Attach an Elastic IP to the instance and a bucket policy allowing access only from that IP.
cards.why: The aws:sourceVpce condition ties access to one VPC; IAM roles, security groups and Elastic IPs can be reproduced or are not valid bucket policy sources.

cards.scenario: New instance Y in a custom security group cannot be pinged by other instances in the VPC.
cards.ok: The default security group allows inbound traffic from instances in the same group; a newly created group allows no inbound traffic.
cards.bad: The default security group allows no inbound traffic from instances in the same group; a newly created group allows all inbound.
cards.why: The default SG has a self-referencing inbound rule, while a new security group starts with no inbound rules, so ICMP must be explicitly added.

cards.scenario: Block specific countries at ALB with WAF but allow remote developers from a blocked country.
cards.ok: Use a WAF geo match statement for the blocked countries and a WAF IP set statement allowing developer IPs.
cards.bad: Use an ALB geo match statement for the blocked countries and an ALB IP set statement allowing developer IPs.
cards.why: Geo match and IP set are AWS WAF rule statements, not ALB features; NACLs on EC2 instances cannot filter by country.

cards.scenario: Copy KMS-encrypted Redshift snapshots from eu-west-1 to another Region for DR.
cards.ok: Create a snapshot copy grant in the destination Region for a KMS key there, then enable cross-Region snapshots in the source Region.
cards.bad: Create a snapshot copy grant in the source Region for a KMS key there, then enable cross-Region snapshots in the destination.
cards.why: KMS keys are Region-specific, so the grant must reference a destination-Region key; copying is configured on the source cluster.

cards.scenario: Secure ElastiCache Redis cluster mode on port 6379 against unauthorized access (select three).
cards.ok: Security group allowing inbound 6379 from cluster and clients, in-transit plus at-rest encryption, and a Redis auth-token on all commands.
cards.bad: CloudTrail for API monitoring, CloudWatch Logs for credentials, and an outbound security group rule to clients on 6379.
cards.why: Access control needs inbound SG rules, encryption and auth token; CloudTrail and logs only monitor, and clients need no outbound rule from the cluster.

cards.scenario: Revamp security after DDoS: static images, EC2 website, RDS database (select two).
cards.ok: Use Route 53 for traffic distribution and put static content in S3 behind CloudFront with AWS WAF.
cards.bad: Use Global Accelerator for traffic distribution and put the ASG behind AWS WAF.
cards.why: Route 53 and CloudFront absorb DDoS at the edge with built-in mitigation and WAF at edge locations; Inspector and Security Hub do not mitigate DDoS.

cards.scenario: Many apps read S3 data lake buckets with tighter access rules and no internet access, most efficiently.
cards.ok: Access points per bucket, apps in one data lake VPC, gateway endpoint allowing only access points, bucket policy denying outside VPC.
cards.bad: Per-application gateway endpoints allowing an access point, per-account access points, and a bucket policy requiring access points.
cards.why: One data lake VPC with one gateway endpoint and a VPC-restricting bucket policy is simplest; interface endpoints are not used for S3 gateway attachment and per-app endpoints add overhead.

cards.scenario: 500 HTTPS apps behind ALBs moving to multi-Region without interrupting HTTPS.
cards.ok: Request a separate ACM certificate per FQDN in each Region and attach to that Region's ALB.
cards.bad: Request one ACM certificate per FQDN and attach the same certificate to ALBs in all Regions.
cards.why: ACM certificates are Regional and cannot be reused across Regions; KMS does not issue SSL/TLS certificates.

cards.scenario: Detect public S3 objects, notify governance team immediately, and auto-remediate (select two).
cards.ok: Object-level logging with an EventBridge rule on public PutObject sending to SNS, plus a Lambda subscriber that secures the objects.
cards.bad: Object-level logging with S3 event notifications triggering Lambda to send SNS notifications about public PutObject.
cards.why: CloudTrail data events matched by EventBridge detect public-read PutObject; S3 event notifications do not expose ACL details, and Trusted Advisor or Access Analyzer are not immediate.

cards.scenario: Auditable, secure patching of mixed Windows and Linux fleet with MINIMAL effort.
cards.ok: Use Systems Manager Agent with maintenance window tasks and approvals, applying baselines via the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document.
cards.bad: Use OS-native patching services with AWS Config for audit and compliance reporting on all instances.
cards.why: Systems Manager Patch Manager handles both OS types with built-in compliance reporting; AWS-RunPatchBaseline is the real document name, not ApplyPatchBaseline.

cards.scenario: Serverless image app shows 504 Gateway Timeout errors; DynamoDB metrics are fine; find root cause.
cards.ok: Analyze Lambda CloudWatch Logs for image processing times and analyze AWS X-Ray traces of HTTP calls.
cards.bad: Enable API Gateway access logging and analyze the access logs for HTTP errors.
cards.why: Lambda logs expose processing time and X-Ray traces show where latency occurs; API Gateway access or execution logs only record requests and errors, not downstream cause.

cards.scenario: Redesign to serverless planned within 6 months; cut costs of current web, app and RDS stack reliably.
cards.ok: On-Demand Instances for the web and application tiers and Reserved Instances for the database tier.
cards.bad: Reserved Instances for the web and application tiers and On-Demand Instances for the database tier.
cards.why: Web and app tiers will be retired within 6 months so no long commitment; the database persists, so reserve it; Spot is unreliable.

cards.scenario: Continuously assess, audit and monitor resource configurations for compliance in regulated industries (select two).
cards.ok: AWS Config managed and custom rules with periodic and change-triggered evaluation, plus CloudTrail across all accounts logging to CloudWatch Logs with KMS.
cards.bad: EventBridge-triggered Lambda auto-reverting changes, plus SDK logs collected with a CloudWatch Logs agent and metric filters.
cards.why: Config rules assess configuration compliance and CloudTrail audits management activity; the other options rely on custom revert code or SDK logs and are not suited to console use.

cards.scenario: Provision Beanstalk environment each morning and terminate at day end; minimal overhead and lowest cost, shared across teams.
cards.ok: Lambda functions with an execution role create and terminate the environment, triggered by EventBridge cron rules.
cards.bad: An EC2 Micro instance with an instance profile role runs cron scripts to create and terminate the environment.
cards.why: Serverless scheduling with EventBridge and Lambda has no server to run or maintain; a cron EC2 instance adds cost and overhead.

cards.scenario: 5 GB upload over internet using S3 Transfer Acceleration that gave no speedup; which charges apply?
cards.ok: No transfer charges, since data into S3 is free and S3TA charges only for accelerated transfers.
cards.bad: Only S3 transfer charges apply to the upload, since the upload was not accelerated.
cards.why: Inbound transfer from the internet to S3 is free, and S3TA bills only when the transfer is actually accelerated.

cards.scenario: Permanently record all traffic to ALB-fronted web app protected by WAF, after instances rebooted and lost logs.
cards.ok: Send WAF web ACL logs to Kinesis Data Firehose, store in S3, and query with Athena.
cards.bad: Send WAF web ACL logs to CloudTrail with an all-Region trail to S3, and query with Athena.
cards.why: WAF logs go to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose, not CloudTrail; VPC Flow Logs do not stream directly to Kinesis Data Streams.

cards.scenario: SNS to Lambda notifications go undelivered at 5000 requests per second during peak season.
cards.ok: SNS deliveries exceed the Lambda account concurrency quota, so request a limit increase from AWS Support.
cards.bad: SNS hit its own concurrency limit, so contact AWS Support to raise the account limit.
cards.why: Lambda concurrency (1000 per Region by default) throttles deliveries; SNS and Lambda are managed services where you cannot provision more servers.
